quiz.p: What is most of the solid part of soil made of?
quiz.why: Most of the solid part of soil is rock broken into sand, silt and clay. Humus from dead plants is a smaller part, and water fills some of the gaps.

quiz.p: Meena, a girl in Class 3, shakes pot soil in a jar of water and puts it down. Which layer reaches the bottom first?
quiz.why: Sand grains are the biggest and heaviest, so they sink in seconds. Clay grains are so small they take a day or more. Humus bits often float.

quiz.p: Kavya's soil jar is still cloudy the next morning. What is making it cloudy?
opts: Clay grains, which are tiny and sink very slowly
quiz.why: Clay grains are the smallest grains in soil. Water can hold them up for a day or longer, which keeps the water cloudy.

opts: From dead plants and animals that decomposers have broken down
quiz.why: Humus is the dark part of soil made when fungi, bacteria, earthworms and other decomposers break down dead leaves, roots and animals.

quiz.p: How does humus help a plant?
opts: It holds water like a sponge and gives nutrients
It keeps the sunlight off the roots
quiz.why: Humus soaks up water and holds it near the roots. As it breaks down further, it releases nutrients that plants need.

quiz.p: A peepal plant grows in a crack in an old wall. What happens to the wall over many years?
opts: The roots grow thicker and push the crack wider
The wall turns into a tree
quiz.why: Roots grow thicker as the plant grows, and they push with great force. This is one way rock and stone are broken up by living things.
Earthworms have no lungs. Air passes in through their skin, but only when the skin is damp. Their slime keeps it damp.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 3, pours water on two cups of packed soil. One cup has pencil holes. What happens?
opts: The cup with holes soaks up the water much faster
Both soak it up at the same speed
The cup with holes keeps a puddle on top
quiz.why: The holes are open paths, like worm tunnels. Water runs down them quickly. On packed soil with no holes, the water sits on top.

quiz.p: Why do farmers like earthworms in their fields?
opts: Worm tunnels let in air and water, and their castings are rich in nutrients
quiz.why: Worm tunnels help air and rain into the soil and give roots easy paths. Worm castings hold nutrients plants can use.

quiz.p: Which crop grows well in the black soil of the Deccan?
quiz.why: Black soil holds water for a long time, which suits cotton. It is also called black cotton soil.

quiz.p: Why is the red soil of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka red?
opts: It has iron in it, the same way rust is red
Red flowers have rotted into it
quiz.why: Red soil holds iron. Iron that has joined with oxygen, like rust, is red.

quiz.p: Why is soil that washes away in a storm such a big loss?
opts: New soil takes hundreds of years to form
The rain takes the soil to the Moon
quiz.why: Soil forms very slowly from rock and dead plants. It can take up to a thousand years to make one centimetre. Soil lost in a storm cannot be quickly replaced.

items.p: The biggest grains in soil, which feel gritty, are called ____.
items.why: Sand grains are the biggest grains in soil. You can see each one, and they feel gritty when rubbed.

items.p: Sort these parts of soil. Did each one come from rock, or from living things?
items.a: see items
items.why: Sand, silt and clay are rock broken very small. Humus and dead roots come from plants. Worm castings are soil that has passed through a worm, so they are made by a living thing, though they also hold rock grains. A strong sorter can explain the castings either way.

items.p: Draw your soil jar the day after you shook it. Label the sand, the silt, the clay, the water and the floating bits.
items.a: Sand at the bottom, then a finer silt layer, then a thin clay layer, then water that is clearer, with dark bits floating at the top.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the layers in the right order and labels each one.
items.art: An empty outline of a tall jar with a lid.

items.p: In the soil jar, sand sank in seconds but clay took a whole day. Why?
items.a: Sand grains are big and heavy, so they sink fast. Clay grains are tiny and light, so the water holds them up for a long time.
items.why: A strong answer links the speed of sinking to the size of the grains.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, finds that lots of dark bits float on her soil jar. What does this tell her?
opts: Her soil has a lot of plant material
Her soil is very old rock
items.why: The floating bits are pieces of dead plants. Lots of them means her soil has a lot of humus, or a lot of cocopeat if it came from a nursery mix.

items.p: Rock can be broken up by plant roots.
items.why: True. Roots grow into cracks and get thicker, which pushes the rock apart.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the slow breaking up of rock
the dark part of soil made from dead plants
soil that comes out of an earthworm
a plant farmers grow in large amounts
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words are used all through the unit.

items.p: An earthworm has no lungs. How do they breathe, and why must their skin stay damp?
items.a: They breathe through their skin. Air can only pass through skin that is damp, so their slime keeps the skin wet.
items.why: A strong answer says skin, and links dampness to breathing.

items.p: Label the earthworm: rings, bristles, slimy skin, mouth end.
items.a: The mouth is at the pointed front end. The body is made of rings. Tiny bristles stick out from each ring. The whole body is covered in slimy skin.
items.why: Each part helps the worm live in soil: rings and bristles for moving, slime for breathing.
items.art: An unlabelled drawing of an earthworm with four blank label lines.

items.p: In the Worm Tunnels test, why did we pack both cups of soil the same?
opts: So that only the tunnels were different
So that the water would go cold
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one cup were packed harder, we could not tell whether the tunnels or the packing made the difference.

items.p: Sort these crops by the soil they grow best in.
items.a: see items
items.why: Cotton likes the water-holding black soil. Ragi and groundnut grow well in red soil. Rice and wheat grow in river plains and deltas.

items.p: Rain or wind carrying soil away is called soil ____.
items.why: Soil erosion is the loss of soil, washed away by rain or blown away by wind.

items.p: Arjun says, "Rocks never change." Give one piece of evidence from your home or this unit that rocks do slowly change.
items.a: Old stone steps are worn smooth in the middle. Chalk pieces shaken in a box lost their corners and made powder. River pebbles are round.
items.why: A strong answer gives something the child can see, and says how it shows the rock is wearing away.

items.p: All soil in India is the same.
items.why: False. India has red, black, river and laterite soils, from different rocks and climates, and they suit different crops.

items.p: Draw a cut-away of soil under a tree. Show fallen leaves on top, humus below them, an earthworm tunnel and a root.
items.a: Leaves on the surface, a dark humus layer below, a worm in a tunnel, and a root growing down.
items.why: A strong drawing shows how dead leaves become humus and how worms and roots share the soil.
items.art: An empty box with a line across it for the ground and a tree trunk at one side.

items.p: Your soil jar settled into layers. Use the layers to explain why soil is a mix and not one material.
items.a: If soil were one material, it would all sink or float together. Instead, sand, silt and clay settled at different speeds, and plant bits floated. So soil is made of different parts mixed together.
items.why: A strong answer uses the different settling speeds as evidence for a mix.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 4, tests two soils in jars. Soil A has a thick sand layer and almost no clay. Soil B has a thick clay layer. Which soil will water drain through faster?
items.why: Sand grains are big, with big gaps between them, so water runs through fast. Clay grains are tiny, with tiny gaps, so water moves slowly and is held.

items.p: Put the journey of a grain in order, from rock to rice field.
items: Sun and rain crack a rock on a hill
A piece breaks off and rolls into a river
The river knocks it into tiny grains
The river lays the grains down in a delta
Worms and roots mix the grains with humus
a: Sun and rain crack a rock on a hill
A piece breaks off and rolls into a river
The river knocks it into tiny grains
The river lays the grains down in a delta
Worms and roots mix the grains with humus
items.why: This is how much of the river soil in the Kaveri and Godavari deltas was made: weathering, then rivers carrying and breaking the grains, then laying them down, then living things making it into topsoil.

items.p: A family on a hill farm is deciding what to do with a bare, steep field before the monsoon.

views.says: Plough it now, so it is ready to plant as soon as the rain comes.
Leave the dry stalks and weeds on it until the rain, so the roots hold the soil.
Build low stone walls across the slope, so the water slows down. It is hard work, but it lasts for years.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason about erosion, such as roots holding soil or walls slowing water, and admits a fair point from another side, such as the need to plant on time.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Each idea weighs work, time and the risk of losing topsoil.

items.p: Ayesha, a girl in Class 3, cuts open old worm tunnels in a field and finds roots growing down inside them. Why do roots grow there?
opts: The soil in a tunnel is loose and has air and water
The tunnels are full of sunlight
items.why: Worm tunnels are open paths, with air, water and castings rich in nutrients. A root senses these and grows where it is easiest and best.

items.p: Earthworms move away from a bright torch held over their soil. How does this help them live?
items.a: In bright light they are easy for birds to see, and sun dries their skin, and they need damp skin to breathe. Moving away from light keeps them safe and damp.
items.why: A strong answer links the behaviour to the worm's problem: drying out and being seen.

items.p: Worm castings hold more nutrients plants can use than the soil the worm swallowed.
items.why: True. Inside the worm, dead plant bits are ground up and partly digested, so nutrients come out in a form plants can use.

items.p: A grain of clay is much ____ than a grain of sand.
items.why: Clay grains are the smallest grains in soil. Hundreds could fit across one sand grain.

items.p: Why does the black soil of the Deccan crack open in summer?
opts: It has lots of clay, which swells when wet and shrinks as it dries
The cotton roots pull it apart
items.why: Clay soaks up water and swells, then shrinks as it dries. Black soil is full of clay, so the shrinking opens deep cracks.

items.p: Match each soil to where in India much of it is found.
pairs: the Ganga plains and the river deltas
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each soil formed from the rock and the weather in its own region.

items.p: Draw two hill slopes after heavy rain: one bare and one with plants. Show what the rain does to each.
items.a: On the bare slope, brown water and soil run down. On the planted slope, the water is clearer and soaks in around the roots.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that roots and plant cover hold soil and slow the water.
items.art: Two empty hill outlines side by side.

items.p: Sort these ways rock is broken up.
items: a root growing in a crack
an earthworm grinding grains in their gut
items.a: see items
items.why: Rock is broken by weather, by living things, and by moving water. Earthworms grind soil grains a little in their gut, so they belong with living things.

items.p: In the Rock to Grains test, what did the white powder at the bottom stand for?
opts: The silt and clay that rocks break into
items.why: The powder was tiny grains knocked off the chalk, like the silt and clay knocked off stones in a river.

items.p: Many people think plants eat soil to grow. Use what you know to say what plants really take from the soil.
items.a: Plants take water and small amounts of nutrients from the soil, and the soil holds them up. Most of a plant's body is made from air and water, joined together using sunlight.
items.why: A strong answer separates what comes from soil, water and nutrients, from what comes from air and light.

items.p: Label the layers in the side of a dug pit: topsoil, lower soil, broken rock, solid rock.
items.a: Dark topsoil at the top, lighter lower soil below it, broken rock below that, and solid rock at the bottom.
items.why: The layers show soil forming from rock below and humus from above.
items.art: An unlabelled drawing of the side of a pit with four bands, darkest at the top and solid grey rock at the bottom.

items.p: A city is deciding what to do with the fallen leaves in its parks.

views.says: Sweep them up and burn them. The park looks tidy, and there are fewer mosquitoes.
Leave them under the trees, or compost them. They are the trees' own food for the soil.

views.who: Kiran, who lives next to the park
views.says: Compost them in a corner of the park, so the paths stay clean and the soil still gets them.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use evidence from this unit. Then say what the other side has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses humus as evidence: fallen leaves become humus that holds water and feeds the soil, and burning sends them into the air as smoke. It also admits a real point on the other side, such as tidy paths.
items.why: This is a real choice that cities make. Each view balances tidiness, smoke and soil.

items.p: Darwin found that earthworms slowly buried stones in a field under their castings. Explain how worms could bury a stone without ever moving it.
items.a: Worms eat soil from under and around the stone and leave castings on the surface. The ground under the stone is tunnelled, so the stone slowly sinks, while castings pile up on top. Over many years, the stone ends up below the surface.
items.why: A strong answer uses both parts of the worms' work: removing soil below and adding castings above.

items.p: Meera, a girl in Class 4, shakes two soils in jars. Jar 1 has 4 cm of sand and 1 cm of clay. Jar 2 has 1 cm of sand and 4 cm of clay. Which soil would crack in the summer heat?
items.why: Clay swells when wet and shrinks when dry, so soil full of clay cracks as it dries. Sandy soil does not shrink much. That is why the clayey black soil of the Deccan cracks.

items.p: One centimetre of soil can take hundreds of years to form. A storm can wash away a centimetre in a day. What does this mean for how we should treat soil?
items.a: Soil we lose cannot be replaced in our lifetime, so we should protect it: keep plants on the ground, put back humus, and stop rain washing it off bare slopes.
items.why: A strong answer compares the two speeds and draws a practical conclusion.

items.p: Earthworms help the soil everywhere in the world.
items.why: False. In some northern forests of North America that had no earthworms for thousands of years, worms brought from elsewhere eat the thick leaf layer that forest plants and animals depend on.

items.p: Dokuchaev found similar rocks under very different soils. What did this show?
opts: Rock alone does not explain what soil forms. Climate, living things and time matter too.
Rock has nothing to do with soil
items.why: If rock alone decided the soil, the same rock would always give the same soil. Dokuchaev showed that climate, plants, the shape of the land and time all change the soil that forms.

items.p: Your Worm Tunnels test used pencil holes. In what way is a real worm tunnel different from a pencil hole? Would that make the real soil soak up water even better, or worse?
items.a: A real tunnel is lined with slime and castings, and worms keep making new ones. Worms also pull leaves down and loosen soil around the tunnel. So real soil with worms probably soaks up water even better, and keeps doing it.
items.why: A strong answer names a real difference and reasons about its effect. Any well-argued answer is good.

items.p: Put these grains in order from the biggest to the smallest.
items.why: Pebbles are bigger than sand, sand is bigger than silt, and clay is the smallest. This is also the order they settle in water.

items.p: A farmer near Thanjavur grows rice in the same field every year and never adds manure. What will slowly happen?
opts: The soil will lose nutrients and the crops will get smaller
The soil will turn into rock
items.why: Each harvest carries away nutrients from the field. Without manure, compost or fertiliser to put them back, the soil slowly gets poorer.

items.p: Design a balcony box that turns your family's fallen leaves and peels into humus. Draw it and label how air, water and worms or other decomposers get in.
items.a: A box or bucket with holes for air, a lid against rain, layers of peels and dry leaves, and a tray underneath for drips.
items.why: A strong design gives decomposers food, air, water and shade, the things they need.
items.art: An empty box outline on a balcony floor.

items.p: Soil scientists say a soil forms from its rock, its climate, its living things, the shape of the land, and ____.
items.why: Dokuchaev named these five things. Time matters because soil forms so slowly.

items.p: Sort these into things that add humus to soil and things that take soil away.
items: heavy rain on a bare field
cow dung spread on a field
strong wind on dry, ploughed land

items.p: Label the parts of this drawing of soil up close: sand grain, silt grain, clay, humus, water, air, root hair.
items.a: The largest grains are sand. Smaller grains are silt. The tiny flakes are clay. The dark bit is humus. The gaps hold water drops and air bubbles. A thin root hair passes between the grains.
items.why: Each part has a job. Grains come from rock. Humus comes from dead plants. Water and air in the gaps keep roots alive.

open_questions.q: How many different kinds of living things live in soil?
open_questions.why_open: Most kinds of soil bacteria and fungi have never been grown or named in a laboratory. Scientists find new ones every year.

open_questions.q: How fast does new soil form in different places?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the rock, the climate, the plants and much more. It is hard to measure because it is so slow, and estimates vary a lot.

open_questions.q: Why exactly do earthworms come to the surface after rain?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have several ideas, such as escaping soil with less air, travelling while the ground is wet, or reacting to the drumming of rain. None is proved for every kind of worm.

open_questions.q: How do roots and fungi decide how much to trade with each other?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that plants and fungi trade sugar for nutrients, and that both sides seem to choose partners. How they balance the trade is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the soil jar, Kavya measured 4 cm of sand, 2 cm of silt and 1 cm of clay. How tall were the settled layers in all? Which layer was the biggest?
maths.answer: 7 cm in all. Sand was the biggest layer.
maths.explain: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. So the layers were 7 cm tall. The sand layer, 4 cm, was more than the silt and clay together, which were 3 cm.
maths.why_maths: Adding and comparing the layers shows which part of the soil there is most of.
maths.context: This is about the soil jar, where soil settled into layers of sand, silt and clay.

maths.problem: Draw a bar chart of Kavya's jar: sand 4 cm, silt 2 cm, clay 1 cm. Then Meena's jar from a different pot: sand 2 cm, silt 2 cm, clay 3 cm. Whose soil would hold more water?
maths.answer: Meena's soil, because it has more clay.
maths.explain: The bars show Kavya's soil is mostly sand and Meena's is mostly clay. Clay has tiny gaps that hold water, so Meena's soil holds more.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart lets you compare two soils at a glance, and then reason about what they will do.

maths.problem: In the Worm Tunnels test, the packed cup took 150 seconds to soak up the water. The cup with tunnels took 15 seconds. How many times faster was the cup with tunnels?
maths.explain: 150 divided by 15 is 10. So the tunnels made the water soak in 10 times faster.
maths.why_maths: Dividing tells you how big the difference is, not just that there is one.
maths.context: This is about the Worm Tunnels test, where water was poured on packed soil with and without pencil holes.

maths.problem: Suppose one centimetre of soil takes 500 years to form. How long would 3 centimetres take?
maths.explain: 3 lots of 500 is 1,500. So 3 centimetres would take 1,500 years, longer than most temples in India have stood.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how slowly soil builds up, and why losing it matters.
maths.context: This is about how slowly soil forms. Real times vary from place to place.

maths.problem: In the methi project, the sand pot had 12 seedlings and the soil pot had 14. On day 21, the tallest in sand was 5 cm and the tallest in soil was 11 cm. The seeds sprouted almost equally. So what made the big difference?
maths.answer: The soil, not the sprouting. Almost the same number sprouted, but the soil plants grew more than twice as tall.
maths.explain: 12 and 14 are close, so both pots sprouted well. 11 cm is more than twice 5 cm. The difference came after sprouting, once the seed's own food was used up and the plants needed the soil's water and nutrients.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two sets of numbers shows which difference is big and which is small, so you can find the real cause.
maths.context: This is about the three-week project growing methi in sand and in soil with compost.

roots.context: We have shaken soil in a jar, made worm tunnels and looked at where soil comes from. Now we ask what soil tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In your jar, the soil split into layers. Sand sank first, fine clay stayed cloudy for a day, and dead plant bits floated. The grains are rock broken very small, and the floating bits were once alive. So the ground under every crop is old rock and old life mixed together.
deep_truth.habit: We call soil dirt, as if it were one plain, worthless material. The jar shows it is two very old things mixed: mountains broken down over centuries, and plants and animals who lived and died there.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Soil Jar, sand settled within a minute, silt within half an hour and clay by the next day, while dark bits of dead roots and leaves floated on top. In Rock to Grains, knocking chalk made rounded pieces and powder like silt.

three.who_am_i: Your body is built from rice, dal and vegetables that grew in soil, so you are partly made of what the rocks and old leaves gave them.
three.what_is_life: Living things take from the soil while they live, and give their bodies back to it when they die, as humus for the next plants.
three.what_is_this_world: The ground under a city is mountains worn down over millions of years and mixed with the remains of countless living beings.

roots.thread: A rock on a hill and a leaf on a tree look like two separate things. Over hundreds of years, the rock is broken into grains and the leaf decomposes into humus. Earthworms swallow both and mix them in their gut. A rice plant then grows from the mix, and a family eats the rice. The same few materials keep going round, taking a new shape each time.

teachings.teaching: From space came air, from air fire, from fire water, from water earth. From earth came plants, from plants food, and from food the person.
teachings.link: The unit follows the last part of this chain. Rice grows from soil, and food from the rice builds the child's own body.

teachings.teaching: The Earth is my mother, and I am her child.
teachings.link: Soil feeds every crop that feeds us, the way a mother feeds a child. The hymn asks us to treat the ground with the same care.

teachings.teaching: For dust you are, and to dust you will return.
teachings.link: The floating bits in the jar were once living plants returning to soil. Plants and animals, people too, are made from what the soil gives and go back to it.

science.text: The atoms in our bodies were once in soil, water and air, and they will go back there. Atoms are not made or lost, only moved.
Most of the living things in soil, especially bacteria and fungi, have never been named or studied.

other_view.view: Soil is a mix of minerals, water, air and living things. Only the living things in it are alive. The sand and clay are minerals, and calling soil a mother, or alive as a whole, is a picture, not a finding.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home in a city flat, with the materials listed. Choices made: the Soil Jar uses pot soil, which every family with one plant has. Pot soil from nurseries is often part cocopeat, which floats, so the step says that a thick floating layer is still a real result. Clay can take two or three days to settle, so the step says so. Dish-washing liquid is optional. The Worm Tunnels test stands pencil holes in for tunnels, so it needs no live worms, and it asks for dry soil because wet soil drains differently. Chalk stands in for rock in Rock to Grains, and the step says chalk is much softer than most rock. The Worm Window needs real earthworms, which may be hard to find in a city, so it is outside the spine and offers a nursery pack. The methi project warns that both pots look alike for the first week, because seeds carry their own food.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1800s, most scientists thought soil was simply the top layer of rock, crumbled into dust. Some thought the rich black soil of southern Russia, called chernozem, meaning black earth, had been left behind by an ancient sea or by swamps. In 1877 a young geologist, Vasily Dokuchaev, began a study of the black earth for the Free Economic Society in St Petersburg. For several summers he travelled across the black earth lands. He dug pits and studied the soil layer by layer, from the dark top down to the rock below. He found that similar rocks could lie under very different soils, and that the soils changed with the climate and the plants growing there. The black earth was darkest where grasses had grown, died and decomposed for thousands of years, adding humus to the top layers. In 1883 he wrote that a soil forms from its rock, its climate, its living things, the shape of the land and the time it has had. Rock alone could not explain a soil. His work began the science of soils.
how_we_found_out.who: Vasily Dokuchaev, a Russian geologist, working for the Free Economic Society in St Petersburg
how_we_found_out.when: 1877 to 1883 (fieldwork across the black earth, and his book Russian Chernozem)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought soil was just crumbled rock, and some thought the black earth was left by a sea or by swamps. Dokuchaev showed that soil forms from rock together with climate, living things, the shape of the land and time, and that the black earth was dark with humus from grasses.
